parts.name: Honda B16 engine block
parts.what: The B16 block is the main aluminum-alloy structure of Honda’s 1.6-liter DOHC VTEC inline-four. It houses the four cylinders and supports the crankshaft and cylinder head.
parts.why: It keeps the cylinders aligned and carries the loads produced by combustion and the rotating assembly.
parts.where: It forms the lower central structure of the engine. The four cylinder bores are machined into the deck at the top, with the crankcase below.

parts.name: Valves and valve springs
parts.what: Sixteen poppet valves—two intake and two exhaust per cylinder—control the flow into and out of the four combustion chambers. Springs return each valve to its seat.
parts.why: The valves seal the combustion chambers between intake and exhaust events. The springs keep the valves following the camshaft-driven valvetrain.
parts.where: The valves fit into guides in the cylinder head, with their heads facing the combustion chambers and their stems, springs, retainers, and keepers on the upper valvetrain side.
parts.installationReason: Install the sixteen valves into their guides, then fit the springs, retainers, and keepers. The procedural model is an educational layout; exact B16 valve geometry and clearances are not yet verified.

guide.overview: The B16 cylinder head uses four valves per cylinder: two intake valves and two exhaust valves. Each valve is returned to its seat by a coil spring.
guide.operation: The camshaft and valvetrain open the valves at the correct points in the four-stroke cycle. The valve springs close them when the opening force is removed.
guide.construction: This is a procedural educational representation with sixteen valve assemblies. It shows valve heads, stems, coil springs, retainers, and keepers as separate visible features. It is not a factory CAD model.
guide.specifications: Exact B16 variant-specific valve diameters, stem sizes, spring rates, installed heights, seat pressures, and service limits have not been verified and are intentionally omitted.
guide.inspection: Check valve stems, faces, guides, seats, springs, and retainers for wear or damage. Use the correct B16 service manual for stem clearance, spring free length, installed height, and pressure limits.
guide.failureModes: Possible issues include burned or bent valves, worn guides, weak or broken springs, damaged retainers, and poor valve seating. Symptoms and limits depend on the exact B16 variant.

parts.name: Intake and exhaust camshafts
parts.what: The two overhead camshafts operate the intake and exhaust valves.
parts.why: Their lobes determine valve lift and timing.
parts.where: They sit in the cylinder head above the valves.

guide.overview: The B16 uses dual overhead camshafts: one operates the intake valves and the other operates the exhaust valves.
guide.operation: As the crankshaft turns, the timing belt drives the camshafts. Each lobe pushes the valve mechanism to open a valve; the valve spring returns it toward its seat as the lobe rotates away. VTEC changes the effective valve-lift and timing behavior by engaging a different rocker profile under the required operating conditions.
guide.construction: This component uses the two supplied CAD meshes converted from Camshaft 1.obj and Camshaft 2.obj. The original mesh coordinates are preserved rather than repositioning the shafts by guesswork.
guide.specifications: Exact B16 engine-code-specific cam lift, duration, journal dimensions, timing marks, and service limits are not asserted here. These values should be taken from the matching Honda service information.
guide.inspection: Inspect cam lobes and journals for scoring, pitting, discoloration, and abnormal wear. Check oil passages and measure journal diameters and lobe heights against the correct B16 service specifications.
guide.failureModes: Possible issues include worn or scored lobes, damaged journals, oil-starvation damage, incorrect cam timing, and blocked oil feeds. Symptoms and limits depend on the exact B16 variant.

parts.installationReason: Lower the intake and exhaust camshafts into their bearing saddles in the cylinder head. The supplied source meshes are used at their original scene coordinates; their exact variant-specific fit has not been independently measured.

parts.name: Rocker arms and VTEC assembly
parts.what: The B16 VTEC valvetrain uses rocker arms to transfer cam-lobe motion to the valves. The VTEC mechanism hydraulically locks selected rocker arms together so the high-lift cam profile can control valve motion.
parts.why: The rocker arms transmit camshaft movement to the valves. VTEC changes which rocker profile controls the valves, allowing different lift and duration behavior.
parts.where: The rocker assemblies sit in the cylinder head between the camshaft lobes and valve stems, with separate intake and exhaust rocker groups.

guide.overview: The B16 VTEC system uses rocker arms for the intake and exhaust valve groups. The center rocker follows the high-lift cam lobe; the VTEC locking mechanism can couple the rocker group so the high-lift profile controls valve motion.
guide.operation: At lower engine speeds, the primary and secondary rocker fingers follow their respective cam profiles. When commanded and sufficient oil pressure is available, a hydraulic pin slides to couple the rocker fingers. The linked group then follows the high-lift cam profile. Exact engagement strategy depends on the B16 variant.
guide.construction: This procedural educational model represents rocker fingers, cam-contact pads, valve-contact pads, pivot bosses, and simplified VTEC locking-pin details. It is not a factory CAD reproduction.
guide.specifications: Exact B16 variant-specific rocker dimensions, pin clearances, oil pressure thresholds, engagement rpm, and service limits are omitted because they have not been verified against a matching Honda service manual.
guide.inspection: Inspect rocker contact surfaces, pivots, locking pins, and oil passages for scoring, wear, sticking, or blocked oil feed. Confirm variant-specific limits using the correct Honda service information.
guide.failureModes: Possible issues include worn rocker contact surfaces, sticking or worn locking pins, restricted oil feed, and failure to engage VTEC. Symptoms and diagnostic thresholds depend on the exact B16 variant.

parts.installationReason: Fit the rocker assemblies after the camshafts are in position. The procedural model illustrates the primary, secondary, and center high-lift rocker fingers and a simplified VTEC locking-pin detail.

parts.name: Camshaft caps
parts.what: The camshaft caps clamp the camshaft journals into the cylinder head's machined bearing saddles.
parts.why: They retain the camshafts in alignment while allowing the journals to rotate on a controlled oil film.
parts.where: Five cap stations are shown along each of the two camshaft galleries, above the camshaft journals.

guide.overview: The camshaft caps secure the camshafts in the cylinder head.
guide.operation: The caps clamp the camshaft journals into the matching bearing saddles. A thin oil film separates the rotating journals from the bearing surfaces during operation.
guide.construction: This educational model shows ten cap bridges, five per camshaft gallery, with bearing-contact details and fasteners. It is a simplified visual representation rather than a factory CAD reproduction.
guide.specifications: Cap locations, dimensions, bolt torque, tightening sequence, and journal clearances vary by B16 variant and must be taken from the matching Honda service manual. Do not use this model for machining or assembly measurements.
guide.inspection: Inspect each cap and its matching cylinder-head saddle for scoring, cracks, damage, and blocked oil feeds. Keep caps in their original numbered positions and orientation.
guide.failureModes: Incorrect cap position, damaged threads, uneven tightening, or poor oil supply can cause camshaft binding and journal damage.

parts.installationReason: Install the camshaft caps after both camshafts are seated in the cylinder-head bearing saddles. The model represents five cap stations on each camshaft.
